Lab 1 · Foundation

The Law of Large Numbers (LLN)

As the number of independent trials $n$ grows, the sample proportion $\hat{p}_n = \frac{H}{n}$ converges almost surely to the theoretical probability $p$. In small samples, streaks and wild swings are common; over large samples, random fluctuations cancel out with mathematical certainty.

Intuition: The dashed orange line represents theoretical $p$. The shaded band shows the 95% error margin $\pm 1.96 \sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$. Notice that while the percentage deviation shrinks towards 0 as $n \to \infty$, the absolute difference $|H - n \cdot p|$ typically grows as $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n})$!
Lab 2 · Physics Simulation

The Galton Board (Quincunx / Bean Machine)

Invented by Sir Francis Galton in 1873 to demonstrate the Central Limit Theorem. As thousands of individual marbles tumble through triangular rows of pegs, each independent left/right deflection accumulates into an exact Binomial distribution $B(R, p)$ that smoothly morphs into the Gaussian Bell Curve.

10
Gaussian Fit R²
> 0.98
Number of Peg Rows (R) 10
Rightward Deflection Bias (p) 0.50
Simulation Speed Fast
💡
Physics to Mathematics: Each marble makes $R$ independent binary decisions. Landing in bin $k$ requires choosing "Right" exactly $k$ times and "Left" $R-k$ times. The probability of landing in bin $k$ is given exactly by the binomial coefficient: $P(X=k) = \binom{R}{k} p^k (1-p)^{R-k}$.
Lab 3 · Limit Theorem

Sum of Random Variables & The Central Limit Theorem

The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) states that the sum (or average) of $k$ independent and identically distributed random variables approaches a Normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$, regardless of the underlying distributions shape. Watch a flat uniform die or a skewed distribution transform into a bell curve!

Lab 4 · Conditional Paradox

The Monty Hall Paradox

You are on a game show with 3 doors. Behind one is a Sports Car 🚗; behind the other two are Goats 🐐. You choose a door. The host, Monty, who knows what is behind every door, opens one of the remaining doors to reveal a goat. He then asks: "Do you want to switch doors?" Should you switch?

Why Switching Doubles Your Odds: Your initial pick has a $1/3$ chance of hiding the car, meaning there is a $2/3$ chance the car is behind one of the other two doors. Montys goat reveal gives you new information by eliminating the losing door among the two. The full $2/3$ probability is transferred to the single unopened door!
Lab 5 · Bayesian Reasoning

Bayes Theorem & The Base Rate Fallacy

If a medical test is 99% accurate and you test positive, what is the probability that you are actually sick? Counter-intuitively, if the disease is rare (e.g. 1 in 1,000), the answer is only ~9%! Because healthy people vastly outnumber sick people, false positives drastically overwhelm true positives.

1,000-Person Population Matrix (Hover dots to inspect individual clinical outcomes)
True Positive (10) False Positive (99) False Negative (0) True Negative (891)
Posterior P(Sick | +)
9.17%
Total Positive Tests
109
False Discovery Rate
90.83%
Disease Prevalence P(D) 1.0%
Test Sensitivity P(+ | D) 99%
Test Specificity P(- | ¬D) 90%
Bayes Formula:
P(D|+) = [P(+|D)·P(D)] / P(+)
= (0.0099) / (0.1089)
💡
The Takeaway: Never interpret test accuracy in a vacuum without the base rate (prior probability). Even with an exceptionally accurate test, when screening for rare conditions, the majority of positive results will still be false alarms!
Lab 6 · Combinatorics

The Birthday Paradox & Hash Collisions

How many people must be in a room before there is a >50% chance that two share the exact same birthday? Most people guess 183 (half of 365). The real answer is just 23 people! With 70 people, the chance reaches 99.9%. This fundamental principle governs hash table collisions and cryptographic security.

Room Size (N)
23
Pairs Compared &binom;(N, 2)
253
Theoretical P(≥ 1 match)
50.73%
Number of People in Room (N) 23
Why 23?
We compare every pair: $\binom{23}{2} = 253$ distinct pairings! The probability that none match is:
P(No Match) = 365/365 × 364/365 × ... × 343/365 ≈ 49.27%
Therefore: $P(\ge 1) = 1 - 0.4927 = 50.73\%$.
💡
Human Intuition Trap: We intuitively ask: "What are the odds someone shares MY birthday?" (which requires 253 people for 50%). But the paradox asks if ANY two people share a birthday, which scales quadratically $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ with the number of pairs!
Lab 7 · Geometric Probability

Buffons Needle (π via Monte Carlo)

In 1777, Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon proved that if a needle of length $L$ is dropped onto floorboards of width $D$ ($L \le D$), the probability that the needle intersects a line is exactly $P = \frac{2L}{\pi D}$. Dropping needles allows you to calculate the digits of $\pi$ through pure physical randomness!

The Formula: Rearranging Buffons equation yields $\pi \approx \frac{2L \cdot N_{\text{total}}}{D \cdot N_{\text{cross}}}$. Cyan needles cross a boundary line; slate needles do not.
Lab 8 · Stochastic Processes

Gamblers Ruin & The House Edge

A gambler starts with $\$k$ and bets $\$1$ at each step with win probability $p$ against an adversary (the casino) with goal $\$N$. Even with a minuscule 1% house edge ($p = 0.49$), the absorbing barrier at $\$0$ makes eventual financial ruin virtually certain over time.

$20

$50

88.1%
Simulated Ruin Rate
—
Player Win Probability (p) 0.49 (Roulette)
Gambler Starting Bankroll (k) $20
Target Bankroll (N) $50
💡
Absorbing Markov Chains: The exact probability of bankruptcy is $P(\text{Ruin}) = \frac{(q/p)^N - (q/p)^k}{(q/p)^N - 1}$ where $q = 1-p$. When $p < 0.5$, exponential drift relentlessly drags the gambler towards 0.

Lab 10 · Sampling Models

Marble Urn: Sampling With vs. Without Replacement

Sampling with replacement keeps the urn composition identical on every draw, creating independent events (Binomial / Multinomial). Sampling without replacement removes picked marbles, creating dependent events where probabilities update after every single pick (Hypergeometric distribution).
